name: Asana
desc: Cloud work management software that helps teams plan, track and automate projects and goals, sold by subscription to businesses.
markets: Paying business customers in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific; offices in the US, Europe, Japan and Australia.
rationale: B2B software brand that could use F1 hospitality and team-operations storytelling to reach enterprise buyers in key markets.
changed: Direct listing on the NYSE in 2020

name: monday.com
desc: Cloud work management platform used by businesses to build workflows for projects, CRM, software development and service operations.
markets: Customers worldwide, strongest in the US and Europe; offices in Israel, the US, Europe, Australia and Asia.
rationale: Heavy brand advertiser selling to businesses globally; F1 offers global reach, B2B hospitality and a workflow technology showcase.
changed: IPO on Nasdaq in 2021

name: NotCo
desc: Food technology company using artificial intelligence to develop plant-based milk, mayonnaise, burgers and ice cream sold through retailers.
markets: Sells in Chile, Argentina, Brazil, Mexico and other Latin American markets, plus the US and Canada.
rationale: Consumer food brand strongest in Latin America; F1 is costly relative to its scale, so fit is limited.

name: Zain Group
desc: Mobile telecommunications group providing mobile, broadband, 5G, fibre and enterprise services to consumers and businesses in the Middle East.
markets: Operates in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Jordan, Bahrain, Sudan and South Sudan; earlier sold its African operations.
rationale: Strong Gulf consumer brand and active sports sponsor; Gulf races in Bahrain, Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi give a natural F1 platform.
changed: Rebranded from MTC to Zain in 2007

name: United Internet
desc: Internet group providing mobile, broadband, web hosting, cloud and consumer email through 1&1, IONOS, GMX and WEB.DE.
markets: Mainly Germany and other European countries; IONOS also serves small businesses in the US, Canada and Mexico.
rationale: Large German consumer and SME brands; F1 could support IONOS in Europe and North America, but marketing is mostly domestic.
changed: Its IONOS subsidiary was separately listed in Frankfurt in 2023

name: Zoom Communications
desc: Communications software for video meetings, phone, contact centre, team chat and AI assistant, sold to businesses, schools and consumers.
markets: Customers worldwide across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific, with offices in many countries.
rationale: Globally recognised brand pushing into enterprise phone and contact-centre sales; F1 offers technology showcase and B2B hospitality.
changed: Renamed from Zoom Video Communications to Zoom Communications in 2024

name: Opera
desc: Develops web browsers including Opera, Opera GX and Opera Mini, earning revenue from search partnerships and advertising.
markets: Hundreds of millions of users worldwide, with large user bases in Europe, Africa, Asia and the Americas; offices in Europe, China and Africa.
rationale: Opera GX targets young gamers worldwide; F1 and sim racing audiences overlap, making a consumer marketing tie-in plausible.

name: Everpure
desc: Supplies all-flash enterprise data storage systems, storage subscriptions and data management software to large enterprises and cloud providers.
markets: Enterprise and cloud customers in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific; long a listed company as Pure Storage.
rationale: Enterprise technology brand that has used F1 for data and technology storytelling with a team; strong B2B hospitality fit.
changed: Renamed from Pure Storage to Everpure in February 2026
f1: Mercedes-AMG Petronas F1 Team partner as Pure Storage (long-running deal; 2026 status not confirmed)

name: Elastic
desc: Software company behind Elasticsearch, selling search, observability and security software and Elastic Cloud services to developers and enterprises.
markets: Customers worldwide; operational headquarters in the US and the Netherlands, with offices across Europe and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: Enterprise data and observability vendor; F1 data workloads offer a technology tie-in, though its brand marketing is modest.

name: Fortinet
desc: Cybersecurity company selling FortiGate firewalls, secure networking, endpoint and cloud security products and subscriptions to enterprises and governments.
markets: Enterprises, service providers and governments worldwide across the Americas, Europe, Middle East and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: Rival cybersecurity firms such as CrowdStrike and ThreatLocker sponsor F1; strong fit for B2B hospitality and security showcase.

name: HubSpot
desc: Cloud customer relationship management platform with marketing, sales, service and content tools sold by subscription to small and mid-sized businesses.
markets: More than 200,000 customers in over 120 countries; offices in North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America.
rationale: Global B2B brand marketing to SMBs; rival Salesforce partners in F1, making a brand and hospitality programme plausible.

name: EPAM Systems
desc: Software engineering and digital services firm building platforms and AI solutions for large enterprises in finance, healthcare and retail.
markets: Clients mainly in North America and Europe; delivery centres across Central and Eastern Europe, Asia and Latin America.
rationale: IT services peers such as Cognizant, Globant and DXC sponsor F1; B2B hospitality and engineering showcase fit well.
changed: Restructured operations away from Russia and Belarus from 2022

name: Concord
desc: Independent music company owning recorded music labels, music publishing catalogues and theatrical licensing rights, earning royalties and licensing fees.
markets: Earns royalties worldwide; offices in the US and Europe.
rationale: Owner of music and theatre rights with little consumer brand marketing; F1 fit limited to content or music licensing.
changed: Concord Music Group merged with Bicycle Music in 2015 to form Concord Bicycle Music, now known as Concord

name: DAZN
desc: Sports streaming service offering live and on-demand football, boxing and other sports to subscribers, funded by subscriptions and advertising.
markets: Subscribers in more than 200 markets, with major businesses in Europe, Japan, the Americas and Australia (Foxtel).
rationale: Sports media company already showing F1 in some markets; a deeper partnership could add content and subscriber promotion.
changed: Acquired Eleven Sports in 2024 and Foxtel in 2025
f1: F1 media rights holder in Spain and Japan (broadcaster, not a sponsor)

name: BMG
desc: Music company managing music publishing rights and recorded music catalogues for songwriters and artists, earning royalties and licensing income.
markets: Offices in more than 20 countries across Europe, North America, Asia-Pacific and Latin America.
rationale: Music rights business with low consumer awareness; F1 fit limited to music content and artist tie-ins.
changed: Bertelsmann became sole owner after buying out KKR in 2013

name: The Walt Disney Company
desc: Entertainment group with film studios, ABC and ESPN networks, Disney+ and Hulu streaming, theme parks, cruises and consumer products.
markets: Consumers worldwide, with theme parks in the US, Europe and Asia and streaming in many countries.
rationale: Global consumer brand; ESPN was F1's US broadcaster through 2025 before Apple took US rights, so the media link has ended.

name: Comcast
desc: Media and technology company providing Xfinity broadband and cable, NBCUniversal networks, Peacock streaming, Universal studios and parks, and Sky.
markets: Mainly the US for broadband and NBCUniversal; Sky serves the UK, Ireland, Italy and Germany.
rationale: Sky is F1's main UK and Italian broadcaster; a wider partnership could support Peacock, Universal or Xfinity in the US.
changed: Announced in 2024 a spin-off of most cable networks into Versant
f1: Owns Sky, F1 broadcaster in the UK, Italy and Germany (media rights, not a sponsor)

name: Legendary Entertainment
desc: Film and television production company that develops and co-finances films such as Dune and Godzilla with major studios and streamers.
markets: Films distributed worldwide by partner studios; operations mainly in the US, with a business in China.
rationale: Produces blockbuster films; F1 tie-in limited to branded content or film promotion rather than a sponsorship.
changed: Acquired by Dalian Wanda Group in 2016; current ownership split not confirmed

name: United Group
desc: Telecoms and media group providing mobile, broadband and pay-TV services and operating TV channels in Southeast Europe.
markets: Operates in Serbia, Bulgaria, Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Greece.
rationale: Regional consumer brands and sports broadcasting in the Balkans; F1 reach exceeds its markets, so fit is modest.

name: Universal Music Group
desc: Largest music company, owning record labels such as Republic, Interscope and Capitol, plus music publishing and merchandising businesses.
markets: Operations and artists worldwide; corporate headquarters in Hilversum, Netherlands, operational headquarters in Santa Monica.
rationale: Global artist roster suits F1 entertainment, race concerts and fan content partnerships rather than classic sponsorship.
changed: Listed on Euronext Amsterdam in 2021 after spin-off from Vivendi

name: CIRSA
desc: Gaming and leisure group operating casinos, slot arcades, bingo halls, betting shops and online gaming for adult customers.
markets: Operates in Spain, Italy, Morocco and several Latin American countries including Mexico, Colombia, Peru and Panama.
rationale: Gaming operators sponsor F1, but strict Spanish gambling advertising rules limit what Cirsa could activate.
changed: Listed on the Spanish stock exchanges in 2025; Blackstone remains a large shareholder

name: Take-Two Interactive
desc: Video game publisher behind Rockstar Games, 2K and Zynga, selling titles such as Grand Theft Auto and NBA 2K.
markets: Players worldwide across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific via consoles, PC and mobile.
rationale: Global gaming brands with young audiences; rival EA holds the F1 game licence, so a tie-in would need other titles.
changed: Acquired Zynga in 2022

name: Cologix
desc: Operates network-neutral data centres and interconnection hubs where enterprises, cloud providers and carriers house equipment and connect networks.
markets: Data centres in around 13 US and Canadian markets, including Ashburn, Columbus, Dallas, Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver.
rationale: B2B infrastructure operator without a consumer brand and only North American reach; weak F1 fit.

name: evoke plc
desc: Betting and gaming operator running William Hill, 888 and Mr Green betting, casino and poker brands online and in shops.
markets: Main markets are the UK, Italy, Spain, Denmark and Romania; corporate office in London, development teams in Israel.
rationale: Betting brands sponsor sport heavily; F1 could promote William Hill, but UK gambling advertising rules are tightening.
changed: Renamed from 888 Holdings to evoke in 2024; acquired William Hill's non-US business in 2022

name: TKO Group Holdings
desc: Sports and entertainment company owning UFC and WWE, earning revenue from media rights, live events, sponsorships and licensing.
markets: Events and media audiences worldwide, mainly North America, with events in Europe, the Middle East, Asia and Latin America.
rationale: Peer sports property more than sponsor; F1 tie-ins could be cross-promotion, events or hospitality collaboration.
changed: Formed in 2023 by merging Endeavor's Zuffa (UFC) with WWE

name: Merlin Entertainments
desc: Leisure operator running visitor attractions including Legoland parks, Madame Tussauds, SEA LIFE aquariums, the London Eye and Alton Towers.
markets: More than 130 attractions in over 20 countries across Europe, North America, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East.
rationale: Family consumer brands and attractions in many F1 host countries; ticketing or fan-experience tie-ins plausible.
changed: Taken private in 2019 by Kirkbi, Blackstone and CPP Investments

name: Sea Limited
desc: Internet group owning Shopee e-commerce, Garena online games and the Monee digital financial services business.
markets: Shopee serves Southeast Asia, Taiwan and Brazil; Garena games such as Free Fire are played worldwide.
rationale: Very high awareness in Southeast Asia and Brazil, both F1 host markets; heavy advertiser making F1 plausible.
changed: SeaMoney renamed Monee in 2024

name: TelevisaUnivision
desc: Spanish-language media company operating Univision and Televisa TV networks, ViX streaming and content production for Hispanic audiences.
markets: Audiences in the US and Mexico, with content distributed across Latin America.
rationale: Spanish-language media reaching US and Mexican audiences; media partnership around Mexico City, Miami and Las Vegas races possible.
changed: Formed in 2022 by merging Univision with Grupo Televisa's content business

name: Beast Industries
desc: Media and consumer goods company of YouTuber MrBeast, producing videos and Beast Games and selling Feastables snacks and Lunchly kits.
markets: Video audience worldwide; Feastables and Lunchly sold mainly in US retail, with some international distribution.
rationale: Huge young global audience and retail snack brand; F1 content collaboration could suit both sides' youth audiences.

name: Playtika
desc: Mobile games developer publishing free-to-play social casino and casual titles such as Slotomania, Bingo Blitz and House of Fun.
markets: Players worldwide, mainly North America and Europe; studios in Israel, Europe, North America and elsewhere.
rationale: Game brands matter more than the corporate name, and social casino content limits F1 activation; weak to modest fit.
changed: IPO on Nasdaq in 2021

name: Cirque du Soleil
desc: Produces touring and resident live acrobatic shows such as O, Mystère and Kooza for ticket buyers and corporate event clients.
markets: Resident shows in Las Vegas and touring productions across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East.
rationale: Las Vegas presence and live-show expertise suit F1 race-week entertainment and hospitality collaborations rather than sponsorship.
changed: Restructured under creditor protection in 2020; taken over by lenders led by Catalyst Capital Group

name: Ooredoo
desc: Telecoms group providing mobile, fixed, broadband, data centre and enterprise services to consumers and businesses.
markets: Operates in Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, Iraq, Algeria, Tunisia, Maldives and Palestine, and in Indonesia through Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison.
rationale: Major Gulf brand and sports sponsor; the Qatar Grand Prix and Middle East races offer a home-market F1 platform.
changed: Indosat merged with Hutchison 3 Indonesia in 2022; sold Myanmar business in 2022

name: FC Barcelona
desc: Professional football club competing in La Liga, earning revenue from matchdays, broadcasting, sponsorship and merchandise.
markets: Fan base worldwide; commercial income from sponsors and merchandise sales across Europe, the Americas and Asia.
rationale: A sports property rather than a sponsor; any F1 link would be cross-promotion or co-branding, not a sponsorship purchase.
changed: Member-owned club; sold shares of TV rights and Barça Studios in 2022

name: Pearson
desc: Education company selling assessments, qualifications, English language tests, digital learning and courseware to schools, universities, employers and governments.
markets: Largest markets are the US and UK, with significant business in India, Asia-Pacific and other international markets.
rationale: Education brand with little sports marketing; F1 STEM and skills programmes give a plausible but not obvious fit.
changed: Sold the Financial Times and its Penguin Random House stake in 2015-2020

name: Sonos
desc: Designs and sells wireless speakers, soundbars, subwoofers and headphones for home audio, through retailers and online.
markets: Sold in many countries, mainly North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: Premium consumer audio brand; F1 lifestyle audience fits product marketing, though budget is limited after recent difficulties.

name: Ubisoft
desc: Video game publisher and developer behind Assassin's Creed, Far Cry, Rainbow Six and Just Dance, with studios worldwide.
markets: Players worldwide; development studios across Europe, North America and Asia.
rationale: Global gaming brand with young audience; F1 crossover content plausible, but financial pressure limits sponsorship budgets.
changed: Set up a Tencent-backed subsidiary, Vantage Studios, in 2025

name: Banijay Group
desc: Entertainment group producing and distributing TV formats such as Survivor and MasterChef, and operating Betclic online sports betting.
markets: Production companies in many countries across Europe, the Americas and Asia-Pacific; Betclic in France and other European markets.
rationale: Content producer for broadcasters plus Betclic, a visible European sports sponsor; Betclic gives the clearer F1 angle.
changed: Listed in 2022 via merger with SPAC Pegasus Entrepreneurs as FL Entertainment; renamed Banijay Group in 2024

name: Iliad
desc: Telecoms group selling mobile and broadband services under the Free brand in France, Iliad in Italy and Play in Poland.
markets: Customers in France, Italy and Poland; also owns stakes in other European operators.
rationale: Disruptive consumer telecom brand in three European markets; low sponsorship culture makes F1 plausible but not obvious.
changed: Delisted from Euronext Paris in 2021 after a buyout by Xavier Niel

name: Verizon
desc: Telecoms company providing wireless, Fios fibre, home internet and enterprise network services to consumers and businesses.
markets: Consumer customers in the US; Verizon Business also serves enterprises with networks in many countries.
rationale: Large US sports sponsor; three US Grands Prix and rival T-Mobile's F1 deal make a US-focused programme plausible.
changed: Agreed in 2024 to acquire Frontier Communications

name: Princeton Digital Group
desc: Develops and operates data centre campuses leased to cloud providers and internet companies in Asia.
markets: Data centres in Singapore, China, India, Indonesia, Japan and Malaysia.
rationale: B2B infrastructure with no consumer brand; Singapore Grand Prix hospitality is the only realistic angle; weak fit.

name: Prysmian Group
desc: Makes power transmission, submarine, building and telecom cables and optical fibre for utilities, construction and data centre customers.
markets: Plants and customers across Europe, North America, Latin America, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East and Africa.
rationale: Global B2B industrial with energy-transition story; B2B hospitality fit, but little consumer marketing.
changed: Acquired Encore Wire in the US in 2024

name: Singtel
desc: Telecoms group providing mobile, broadband, TV and enterprise ICT services, with stakes in operators across Asia and Australia.
markets: Singapore and Australia (Optus), plus associates in India, Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines.
rationale: Former Singapore Grand Prix title sponsor; home race and regional reach keep F1 relevant for hospitality and brand.

name: TIM (Telecom Italia)
desc: Telecoms company providing mobile, fixed, broadband and ICT services in Italy and mobile services in Brazil through TIM Brasil.
markets: Customers in Italy and Brazil; Italian fixed network sold in 2024.
rationale: Strong Italian brand and sports sponsor; Monza and Imola races and Brazilian F1 audience give clear platforms.
changed: Sold its fixed network (NetCo) to a KKR-led group in 2024; Poste Italiane became largest shareholder in 2025

name: Swisscom
desc: Telecoms company providing mobile, broadband, TV and IT services in Switzerland and broadband and mobile in Italy via Fastweb.
markets: Customers in Switzerland and Italy, where it merged Vodafone Italia into Fastweb.
rationale: Strong Swiss brand and sports sponsor; Italian reach adds relevance, but there is no Swiss race.
changed: Acquired Vodafone Italia in 2024 and combined it with Fastweb

name: Zain Saudi Arabia
desc: Mobile operator providing mobile, 5G, broadband, fibre, digital payment and cloud services to consumers and businesses in Saudi Arabia.
markets: Customers in Saudi Arabia only; part of the Kuwait-based Zain Group.
rationale: Saudi Arabian Grand Prix and Vision 2030 sports push give a home-market platform; rival STC already partners F1.

name: Airtel Africa
desc: Mobile operator providing voice, data and Airtel Money mobile money services to consumers and businesses in 14 African countries.
markets: Operates in 14 countries in East, Central and West Africa, including Nigeria, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and Zambia.
rationale: Large African consumer brand, but no African Grand Prix currently; F1 reach is poorly matched to its markets.
changed: Listed in London and Lagos in 2019

name: Airalo
desc: Sells eSIM mobile data plans for travellers in about 200 countries through its app and website, with business plans.
markets: Travellers worldwide buying data plans online; company based in Singapore, incorporated in the US.
rationale: Travel-focused digital brand; F1's travelling fan base and global calendar suit a targeted digital campaign.

name: China Mobile
desc: State-controlled mobile operator providing mobile, broadband, 5G, cloud and enterprise services to consumers and businesses in China.
markets: Customers in mainland China and Hong Kong; small international carrier and enterprise business.
rationale: Domestic Chinese state operator; Chinese Grand Prix is its only F1 angle, with state constraints on sponsorship.
changed: Delisted from the NYSE in 2021

name: ZTE
desc: Makes 4G and 5G network equipment, fibre access, routers and consumer devices such as smartphones for carriers and consumers.
markets: Carrier customers in many countries across Asia, Europe, Africa and Latin America; limited US business due to restrictions.
rationale: Global B2B telecoms supplier with consumer phones; US sanctions history and restricted markets reduce F1 appeal.

name: Prysmian (North America)
desc: North American unit of the Prysmian cable group, making power, building and telecom cables for utilities, contractors and network operators.
markets: Customers in the US and Canada; part of Milan-based Prysmian Group, which operates worldwide.
rationale: Subsidiary of an Italian B2B cable maker; any F1 decision would sit with the parent, weak standalone fit.

name: Xiaomi
desc: Makes smartphones, smart home devices, TVs, wearables and electric cars, selling to consumers online and through retail stores.
markets: Sells in over 100 countries across Asia, Europe, Latin America and the Middle East; electric cars sold in China.
rationale: Global consumer brand now making high-performance electric cars; F1 offers automotive credibility and international reach.

name: Samsung Electronics
desc: Makes smartphones, TVs, home appliances, memory chips and display panels for consumers and businesses worldwide.
markets: Sells worldwide across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the Middle East.
rationale: Global consumer brand and Olympic sponsor; rivals such as Lenovo and HP partner F1, an obvious fit.

name: STMicroelectronics
desc: Designs and makes microcontrollers, sensors, power chips and silicon carbide devices for automotive, industrial and consumer electronics customers.
markets: Customers worldwide; manufacturing mainly in France, Italy, Singapore, Malaysia and other Asian countries.
rationale: Major automotive chip supplier; F1 gives a technology showcase and B2B hospitality with carmaker customers.

name: Foxconn (Hon Hai Precision Industry)
desc: Electronics contract manufacturer assembling smartphones, servers and other devices for brands such as Apple, and developing electric vehicle platforms.
markets: Factories in China, India, Vietnam, Mexico, the US and Europe, serving global technology brands.
rationale: B2B manufacturer with little consumer marketing; EV and AI-server ambitions offer a technology angle, modest fit.

name: LG Display
desc: Makes OLED and LCD display panels for TVs, smartphones, monitors, laptops and cars, supplying electronics makers and carmakers.
markets: Customers worldwide; production mainly in South Korea, with further plants elsewhere in Asia.
rationale: B2B component supplier with automotive displays; technology showcase possible, but consumer marketing value is low.

name: Analog Devices
desc: Designs analog, mixed-signal and signal processing chips for industrial, automotive, communications, healthcare and consumer electronics customers.
markets: Customers worldwide across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: Automotive and industrial chip supplier; F1 sensing and data technology tie-in and B2B hospitality plausible.
changed: Acquired Maxim Integrated in 2021

name: Emirates Global Aluminium
desc: Produces primary aluminium at smelters in Abu Dhabi and Dubai and mines bauxite, selling to manufacturers in many industries.
markets: Customers in many countries across Asia, Europe and the Americas; bauxite mining in Guinea and recycling in Germany.
rationale: UAE state-owned industrial with Abu Dhabi race links possible; B2B hospitality and lightweight-materials story, moderate fit.
parent: Mubadala Investment Company and Investment Corporation of Dubai (jointly)
changed: Formed in 2013 from Dubai Aluminium and Emirates Aluminium; acquired Leichtmetall in Germany in 2024

name: Wesco International
desc: Distributes electrical, communications, industrial and utility products and supply chain services to contractors, utilities, data centres and manufacturers.
markets: Mainly the US and Canada, with operations in many other countries.
rationale: B2B distributor with little brand marketing; F1 hospitality could suit key accounts, but fit is weak.
changed: Acquired Anixter in 2020

name: Ceconomy
desc: Parent of MediaMarkt and Saturn consumer electronics retailers, selling electronics and services through stores and online.
markets: More than 1,000 stores in about eleven European countries, led by Germany.
rationale: Large European consumer brand and sports sponsor; European races offer retail promotions, but buyer is changing.
changed: Separated from Metro in 2017; JD.com agreed to acquire it in 2025 (completion not confirmed)

name: Lowe's
desc: Home improvement retailer selling appliances, tools, building materials and garden products to homeowners and contractors through stores and online.
markets: Stores in the United States only after selling its Canadian business in 2022.
rationale: Big US advertiser with past motorsport sponsorship; US Grands Prix allow a domestic programme, but F1 is global.
changed: Sold its Canadian business in 2022

name: Nidec
desc: Makes electric motors, from precision motors for hard drives and appliances to automotive traction motors, industrial drives and machine tools.
markets: Customers and plants worldwide across Asia, Europe and the Americas.
rationale: Global supplier to carmakers and industry; electric drive technology offers an F1 showcase, though consumer marketing is limited.

name: Electrolux
desc: Makes refrigerators, ovens, washing machines, dishwashers and vacuum cleaners sold to consumers under Electrolux, AEG and Frigidaire brands.
markets: Sells across Europe, North America, Latin America and Asia-Pacific, with plants in many countries.
rationale: Household brands in many F1 markets; appliance rivals rarely sponsor F1 and margins are tight, so fit is moderate.
changed: Spun off Electrolux Professional in 2020

name: MediaTek
desc: Fabless chip designer making system-on-chips for smartphones, smart TVs, Wi-Fi routers, IoT devices, Chromebooks and cars.
markets: Sells to device makers in Asia, North America and Europe; offices in many countries.
rationale: Rival Qualcomm's Snapdragon partners F1; MediaTek could use F1 to build its Dimensity and automotive chip brand.

name: ams OSRAM
desc: Makes LEDs, lasers, optical sensors and emitters used in cars, smartphones, industrial and medical equipment.
markets: Customers worldwide, mainly carmakers and electronics firms in Europe, Asia and North America; co-headquarters in Munich.
rationale: Automotive lighting and sensor supplier; F1 offers B2B hospitality and lighting technology showcase, modest consumer value.
changed: ams acquired OSRAM in 2020

name: Asus Global
desc: Singapore-based subsidiary of ASUS, the Taiwanese maker of laptops, desktops, motherboards, monitors and Republic of Gamers gaming hardware.
markets: ASUS products sold worldwide; this Singapore entity is one of the group's subsidiaries, its exact role not confirmed.
rationale: ASUS is a global consumer PC and gaming brand; rivals Lenovo, HP and Dell partner F1, so fit is strong.

name: Emerson
desc: Automation company supplying control systems, valves, measurement instruments, test equipment and industrial software to process and manufacturing industries.
markets: Customers in more than 150 countries across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: Global B2B automation firm; F1 data and engineering showcase plus hospitality is plausible, but consumer value is low.
changed: Acquired NI in 2023 and the rest of AspenTech in 2025

name: Applied Materials
desc: Supplies deposition, etch, implant and inspection equipment and services used by chipmakers and display makers.
markets: Customers in Taiwan, South Korea, China, the US, Japan and Europe.
rationale: Concentrated B2B customer base of chipmakers; little need for mass branding, weak F1 fit beyond hospitality.

name: Sony Group
desc: Conglomerate in PlayStation games, music, films, consumer electronics such as TVs and cameras, and image sensors.
markets: Consumers worldwide across North America, Europe, Japan and the rest of Asia.
rationale: Global consumer brand with gaming and Gran Turismo racing links; F1 fan engagement and product tie-ins make sense.
changed: Spun off Sony Financial Group as a separately listed company in 2025

name: Haier
desc: Appliance group making refrigerators, washing machines and air conditioners under Haier, GE Appliances, Fisher & Paykel and Candy brands.
markets: Sells in more than 160 countries across Asia, North America, Europe and other regions.
rationale: Global appliance brand seeking premium image outside China; F1 could support European and Asian brand building.
changed: Its affiliate Haier Smart Home is listed in Shanghai and Hong Kong

name: Gree Electric Appliances
desc: Makes household and commercial air conditioners, plus other household appliances, sold under Gree and other brands.
markets: Mainly China, with exports to many countries in Asia, Africa, Latin America and elsewhere.
rationale: Mainly domestic brand with export ambitions; the Chinese Grand Prix offers an angle, but fit is not obvious.

name: LG Electronics
desc: Makes TVs, home appliances, air conditioning systems and vehicle components, selling to consumers and businesses.
markets: Sells worldwide across North America, Europe, Asia and Latin America.
rationale: Former F1 global partner (2009-2013); global consumer brand with OLED TVs and EV parts, a strong fit.
changed: Exited smartphones in 2021; listed its Indian unit in 2025

name: Dreame Technology
desc: Makes robot vacuums, cordless vacuums, hair dryers, robotic lawn mowers and other smart home appliances for consumers.
markets: Sells in more than 100 markets in Asia, Europe, North America and other regions.
rationale: Fast-growing consumer brand investing heavily in international marketing; F1 suits premium brand building.

name: TCL Technology
desc: Makes LCD and OLED display panels through TCL CSOT and solar silicon materials through TCL Zhonghuan.
markets: Customers worldwide; TCL TVs and phones are sold by sister company TCL Electronics, not this company.
rationale: B2B display and solar maker; the TCL consumer brand sits mostly in sister TCL Electronics, so fit is moderate.
changed: Moved its consumer electronics businesses to TCL Industries in 2019

name: WEG
desc: Makes electric motors, generators, transformers, drives and automation equipment for industry, energy and infrastructure customers.
markets: Plants in Brazil, other Latin American countries, Europe, Asia, Africa and the US; sells in over 100 countries.
rationale: Global B2B industrial with Brazilian roots; São Paulo Grand Prix and electrification story give a moderate fit.

name: Broadcom
desc: Designs networking, broadband, wireless and custom AI chips and sells infrastructure software including VMware to tech companies and enterprises.
markets: Customers worldwide, concentrated among large technology firms and enterprises in North America, Asia and Europe.
rationale: B2B giant with concentrated customers; VMware enterprise sales could use hospitality, but brand marketing is limited.
changed: Avago Technologies acquired Broadcom Corporation in 2016 and took its name; acquired VMware in 2023

name: Kioxia
desc: Makes NAND flash memory and solid-state drives for data centre, smartphone and PC customers.
markets: Customers worldwide; fabs in Yokkaichi and Kitakami, Japan, run jointly with Sandisk.
rationale: B2B memory maker with limited consumer brand; F1 data and storage tie-in possible but not obvious.
changed: Renamed from Toshiba Memory in 2019; listed in Tokyo in 2024

name: Corsair Gaming
desc: Makes PC gaming and streaming hardware, including memory, cases, cooling, keyboards, mice, headsets and Elgato streaming gear.
markets: Sold through retailers and online in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: Gaming brand overlapping with sim racing and esports; F1 esports or sim tie-ins fit, though budgets are modest.

name: Chint Electric
desc: Makes low-voltage electrical equipment such as circuit breakers, contactors, relays and meters, plus solar and energy storage products.
markets: Mainly China, with sales in many countries across Asia, Europe, Africa and Latin America.
rationale: B2B electrical supplier with growing international sales; F1 would be costly for limited return, weak fit.

name: Gen Digital
desc: Consumer cybersecurity company selling Norton, Avast, AVG, Avira and LifeLock security, privacy and identity protection subscriptions.
markets: Consumers worldwide across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific; co-headquartered in Tempe and Prague.
rationale: Consumer security brands with global reach; cybersecurity rivals sponsor F1, making a brand campaign plausible.
changed: NortonLifeLock merged with Avast and was renamed Gen Digital in 2022; acquired MoneyLion in 2025

name: ASML
desc: Makes photolithography systems, including the only EUV lithography machines, used by chipmakers to produce advanced microchips.
markets: Customers are chipmakers in Taiwan, South Korea, the US, China and Japan.
rationale: Very few customers and no consumer brand; F1 could only aid employer branding, weak fit.

name: Segway-Ninebot
desc: Makes electric kick scooters, self-balancing scooters, e-bikes, mopeds and robotic lawn mowers for consumers and sharing operators.
markets: Sells in North America, Europe and Asia; Chinese parent group is based in Beijing.
rationale: Global consumer mobility brand; motorsport association could support scooters and powersports, a plausible fit.
parent: Ninebot (listed on the Shanghai STAR Market)
changed: Segway acquired by Ninebot in 2015

name: Stanley Electric
desc: Makes automotive lighting such as headlamps and tail lamps, plus LEDs and lighting units for other uses.
markets: Supplies carmakers worldwide; factories and offices in about 18 countries across Asia, North America and Europe.
rationale: B2B auto supplier; Japanese Grand Prix and Honda links give modest hospitality value, little consumer branding.

name: Insta360 (Arashi Vision)
desc: Makes 360-degree and action cameras, small cameras and gimbals for creators, travellers and sports enthusiasts.
markets: Sold online and through retailers worldwide; offices in Los Angeles, Tokyo and Berlin.
rationale: Action camera brand built on sports content; onboard F1 footage and creator content make a natural fit.
changed: Listed on the Shanghai STAR Market in 2025

name: Ningbo Joyson Electronic
desc: Makes steering wheels, airbags, seat belts and automotive electronics for global carmakers through Joyson Safety Systems and other units.
markets: Supplies carmakers worldwide, with plants in Asia, Europe and the Americas.
rationale: B2B auto supplier with safety expertise; F1 safety tie-in possible, but little consumer brand need.
changed: Acquired Key Safety Systems in 2016 and Takata's assets in 2018

name: Roborock
desc: Makes robot vacuums and mops, wet-dry handheld vacuums and other cleaning appliances sold under its own brand.
markets: Sold in more than 100 countries, including China, Europe, North America and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: Fast-growing premium consumer brand expanding abroad; F1 could support brand building in Europe and Asia.

name: Acer
desc: Makes laptops, desktops, monitors and gaming hardware under Acer and Predator brands for consumers, businesses and schools.
markets: Sells in more than 160 countries across Asia, Europe and the Americas.
rationale: Global consumer PC brand; rivals Lenovo, HP and Dell partner F1, so a partnership is plausible.

name: TE Connectivity
desc: Makes connectors, sensors and cable assemblies for cars, industrial equipment, aerospace, medical devices and data networks.
markets: Customers worldwide; operational centre in Pennsylvania and plants across the Americas, Europe and Asia.
rationale: Major automotive component supplier; F1 engineering showcase and B2B hospitality plausible, little consumer branding.
changed: Spun out of Tyco International in 2007 as Tyco Electronics; renamed TE Connectivity in 2011; redomiciled to Ireland in 2024

name: Sembcorp Industries
desc: Energy and urban solutions group producing thermal and renewable power and developing industrial parks.
markets: Operations in Singapore, India, China, the UK, the Middle East, Vietnam and Indonesia.
rationale: Energy group with a Singapore home race; energy-transition messaging possible, but utility fit is weak.
changed: Spun off Sembcorp Marine in 2020

name: E.ON
desc: Energy company operating electricity and gas distribution networks and supplying power, gas and energy services to households and businesses.
markets: Customers in Germany, the UK, the Netherlands, Sweden, Italy, Romania and other European countries.
rationale: Large European energy retailer with sports sponsorship; utility regulation and domestic focus limit F1 fit.

name: Vodafone Group
desc: Telecoms operator providing mobile, broadband, TV and business connectivity services in Europe and Africa, including M-Pesa mobile money.
markets: Operates in Germany, the UK, Turkey and other European countries, and in Africa through Vodacom.
rationale: Former McLaren title sponsor (2007-2013); strong European brand with B2B connectivity, a plausible return to F1.
changed: Sold Spain in 2024 and Italy in 2024; merged UK business with Three in 2025
